claims.claim: Rust with axum fits the resource budget (under 20 MB memory, start-up under 1 s) easily
claims.measured: rust-axum: 1 MB idle, 3–9 MB peak across all tests, 238 ms start-up
claims.why: Peak memory stays well below 20 MB in every test, and start-up is about a quarter of a second.

claims.claim: A release build on the single-threaded tokio runtime would use a few MB of resident memory when idle
claims.measured: 1 MB idle; 3 MB peak in plaintext, JSON and CPU tests; 9 MB peak in I/O and database tests
claims.why: Measured idle and light-load memory is about 1–3 MB, which matches 'a few MB' within a factor of 2.

claims.claim: It starts in milliseconds, so the 1-second requirement comes down to systemd ordering, not the language
claims.why: Measured start-up is a few hundred milliseconds, far inside the 1 s limit, so the language is not the constraint.

claims.claim: A stripped binary with size optimisations is typically a few MB before compression, and compresses to well under a few MB
claims.why: Only full container image sizes are measured (79 MB for axum, including the base image), not binary size.

claims.claim: Go binaries are bigger than Rust's (bad over cellular)
claims.measured: Image size: go-nethttp 85 MB, go-gin 92 MB vs rust-axum 79 MB, rust-actix 83 MB
claims.why: The images point the same way but include base layers, so they don't isolate binary size.

claims.claim: Go's garbage-collected memory use is less predictable against a hard 20 MB cap
claims.measured: go-nethttp peak 7–15 MB across tests, 2 MB idle
claims.why: Peaks are measured, and all stay under 20 MB, but variance over time is not, so 'predictability' can't be checked.

claims.claim: Drogon (and Beast) are heavy for this job
claims.measured: cpp-drogon: 4 MB idle, 6–17 MB peak, 295 ms start-up, 82 MB image
claims.why: If 'heavy' means resource use, Drogon measured among the lightest servers: well under 20 MB, under 300 ms start-up, an image about the size of Rust's.

claims.claim: For Python (FastAPI or Flask), the interpreter and libraries alone are likely to use most or all of the 20 MB
claims.measured: Idle memory: python-fastapi 40 MB, python-flask 115 MB, flask-gthread 52 MB, flask-gevent 60 MB
claims.why: Every Python server is above 20 MB at idle, so 'all of the 20 MB' holds, though the claim understates how far over they are.

claims.claim: For Node.js, the interpreter and libraries alone are likely to use most or all of the 20 MB
claims.measured: Idle memory: node-express 38 MB, node-fastify 43 MB
claims.why: Both Node servers already exceed 20 MB at idle, which agrees with the claim that the runtime uses the whole budget.

claims.claim: Starting Python or Node.js in under a second on a Cortex-A53 is doubtful
claims.measured: Start-up on a fast x86 CPU: python-fastapi 895 ms, python-flask 996 ms, flask-gthread 606 ms, node-express 706 ms, node-fastify 593 ms
claims.why: These already take 0.6–1.0 s on a much faster x86 CPU, so they would very likely exceed 1 s on a Cortex-A53.
